p.src: This gāthā tells how Master Xuanzang attained a thorough understanding of the Heart Sutra and opened the gate to enlightenment. By keeping it ever in his thoughts and constantly reciting it, a spark of spiritual light shone through of itself.

p.src: Now the three travelers journeyed on, eating in the wind and sleeping by the waters, setting out beneath the moon and pressing on under the stars, until before long the burning days of summer came again. There they saw:

u.src: Now the three travelers journeyed on, eating in the wind and sleeping by the waters, setting out beneath the moon and pressing on under the stars, until before long the burning days of summer came again.

p.src: As they traveled that day, evening suddenly fell, and they saw a village dwelling beside the mountain road. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, look: the sun sinks behind the western hills, concealing its fiery mirror, while the moon rises from the eastern sea and reveals its icy disk. Luckily there is a household by the road. Let us ask to stay the night and continue tomorrow.” Bajie said, “Quite right. Old Pig is a little hungry too. Let us go beg some vegetarian food from them; then I shall have the strength to carry the luggage.” The Pilgrim said, “You homesick devil! You have been away from home only a few days, and already you are complaining.” Bajie said, “Brother, I cannot compare with a fellow like you who lives on wind and feeds on mist. In all the days since I began following Master, I have constantly endured a half-empty belly. Do you know that?” Hearing this, Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, if your attachment to home is so strong, you are no true monk. You had better go back.” The fool was so alarmed that he fell to his knees and said, “Master, do not listen to what Elder Brother says. He is deliberately casting blame on me. I never complained about anything, yet he says I did. I am merely a simple, plainspoken fool. I said that I was hungry and that we should find a household where we could beg a vegetarian meal, and he called me a homesick devil. Master, I accepted the Bodhisattva’s discipline and have also received your compassion. I willingly serve you on the journey to the Western Heaven and swear that I shall never turn back or repent. This is what they call ‘embracing hardship in the practice of the Way.’ How can you say that these are not the words of a monk?” Tripitaka said, “If that is so, get up.”

p.src: The fool sprang to his feet. Muttering endlessly under his breath, he shouldered the load and had no choice but to set his heart firmly on the task and follow them onward. They soon arrived before the door of the house beside the road. Tripitaka dismounted, the Pilgrim took the reins, and Bajie set down the luggage; all three stood beneath the green shade. Leaning on his nine-ringed priest’s staff and adjusting his rattan-bound woven-bamboo hat, Tripitaka went first to the door. There he saw an old man reclining on a bamboo couch, softly murmuring the Buddha’s name. Not daring to raise his voice, Tripitaka called gently, “Good patron, I offer my greetings.” The old man tumbled to his feet, hastily straightened his clothes, and came out to return the greeting. “Reverend sir, forgive me for failing to welcome you. From what region have you come? And what brings you to my humble home?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk is a priest from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. By imperial command, I am going to Thunderclap Monastery to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Night overtook us just as we reached your honored region, so we hoped to lodge at your worthy residence for one night. We earnestly beg you to grant us this kindness.” The old man waved his hands and shook his head. “You cannot go there. It is hard indeed to obtain scriptures in the Western Heaven. If you want scriptures, you had better go to the Eastern Heaven.” Tripitaka said nothing, but pondered inwardly, “The Bodhisattva directed me westward; why does this old man tell me to go east? How could there be scriptures in the east?” Too embarrassed to speak, he gave no answer for a long while.

p.src: Now the Pilgrim was fierce and unruly by nature. Unable to restrain himself, he stepped forward and cried, “Old man, you have lived to such an age yet understand nothing at all. We monks have come from afar to ask for shelter, and you try to frighten us with such disheartening talk. Even if your house is so cramped that there is nowhere to sleep, we can spend the night sitting beneath a tree and need not trouble you.” The old man seized Tripitaka and said, “Master, you yourself say nothing, but that disciple of yours—with his crooked face, jutting cheeks, thunder-god’s mouth, and red eyes, looking like a consumptive demon—how dare he insult an old man like me?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Old man, you truly have no eye for quality. Those handsome fellows are what people call pleasant to look at but useless when needed. Old Sun may be small, but I am sturdy enough—a solid bundle of sinew wrapped in skin.” The old man said, “You must possess some abilities, then.” The Pilgrim replied, “I dare not boast, but my skills will pass muster.” The old man asked, “Where is your home? And what caused you to shave your head and become a monk?” The Pilgrim said, “Old Sun’s ancestral home is the Water Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the kingdom of Aolai beyond the Eastern Sea in the Eastern Continent of Superior Body. From childhood I learned the ways of a demon and took the name Wukong. By my own prowess I became the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. But because I refused to submit to Heaven’s register and raised a great rebellion in the Celestial Palace, I brought a calamity upon myself. Now I have escaped tribulation and am atoning for my offenses. I have converted to Buddhism and seek the true fruit of enlightenment. I am escorting this master, a subject of the Tang emperor, to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha. Why should I fear lofty mountains and perilous roads, broad waters and raging waves? Old Sun can catch fiends and subdue demons, tame tigers and seize dragons; I even know a thing or two about kicking Heaven and stirring up wells. If bricks or tiles fly about your residence, pots cry out, or doors open of themselves, Old Sun can soon bring them under control.”

p.src: After hearing this speech, the old man laughed aloud. “So you are merely a glib-tongued mendicant monk who goes about thrusting himself upon people.” The Pilgrim said, “It is your son who is glib-tongued! These days the hardship of traveling with my master has made me too weary even to talk.” The old man said, “If travel had not wearied you and you were not too lazy to speak, you would surely chatter me to death. Since you have such abilities, you may indeed be able to journey west. Yes, you may. How many are in your company? Come and spend the night in my humble cottage.” Tripitaka said, “Many thanks, venerable patron, for your kindness in not turning us away. There are three of us.” The old man asked, “Where is the other one?” Pointing, the Pilgrim said, “Your eyes must be dim, old man. Is that not he standing beneath the green shade?” The old man’s sight was indeed dim. When he raised his head and looked closely, he caught sight of Bajie’s face and was so terrified that he stumbled backward at every step, fleeing wildly into the house and crying, “Shut the door! Shut the door! A monster has come!” The Pilgrim ran after him, caught hold of him, and said, “Do not be afraid, old man. He is no monster; he is my junior fellow disciple.” Trembling all over, the old man said, “Fine, fine, fine! Each monk is uglier than the last.” Bajie stepped forward and said, “Old sir, if you judge people by their looks, you are completely mistaken. Ugly we may be, but we are both useful.”

p.src: As the old man stood before the door talking with the three monks, two young men appeared to the south of the farmstead, returning from planting rice with an old woman and three or four boys and girls. Their clothes were hitched up and their feet were bare. They saw a white horse and a load of luggage before their door, with a noisy crowd gathered there. Not knowing who the visitors were, they all surged forward and asked, “What are you doing here?” Bajie turned his head, flapped his ears several times, and thrust out his long snout. The sight frightened them so badly that they toppled this way and that, staggering and tumbling over one another. In alarm, Tripitaka called out repeatedly, “Do not be afraid! Do not be afraid! We are not wicked men. We are monks going to fetch the scriptures.” Only then did the old man come out. Helping the old woman to her feet, he said, “Get up, wife, and do not be so frightened. This master has come from the Tang empire. His disciples merely have ugly faces; though fierce in appearance, they are kind at heart. Take the boys and girls into the house.” The old woman then took hold of the old man, while the two young men led the children inside.

p.src: Tripitaka sat upon a bamboo bed in the gatehouse and complained, “Disciples, the two of you are ugly in appearance and coarse in speech. You have frightened this entire household half to death and brought sin upon me.” Bajie said, “To tell you the truth, Master, since I began following you, old Pig has grown much handsomer.” “Back in the old days at Gao Village, whenever I thrust my snout forward and flapped my ears from side to side, I would regularly frighten twenty or thirty people to death.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Stop talking nonsense, you idiot. Tidy up some of that ugliness of yours.” Tripitaka said, “Listen to what Wukong is saying! A person’s looks are inborn; how do you expect him to tidy them up?” The Pilgrim said, “Tuck that rake of a snout into your clothes and do not bring it out;” “press those fan-shaped ears back and do not wag them. That is how you tidy yourself up.” Bajie actually tucked in his snout and pressed back his ears, then stood beside them with his head hunched down. The Pilgrim carried the luggage inside and tethered the white horse to a post.

p.src: Only then did the old man return with a young fellow who carried a wooden tray bearing three cups of clear tea to offer them. When they had finished their tea, he ordered that a vegetarian meal be prepared. The young man then brought out an old, unpainted table full of holes and two broken stools with damaged legs, placed them in the courtyard, and invited the three pilgrims to sit in the shade. Tripitaka then asked, “May I ask your honorable surname, good patron?” The old man replied, “My surname is Wang.” “How many sons do you have?” He replied, “I have two sons and three young grandsons.” Tripitaka said, “Congratulations, congratulations.” He asked again, “And how old might you be?” The old man replied, “I have foolishly lived to the age of sixty-one.” The Pilgrim said, “Excellent, excellent, excellent! You have begun your second cycle of sixty years.” Tripitaka asked once more, “Good patron, why did you say at first that the scriptures in the Western Heaven would be difficult to obtain?” The old man replied, “It is not the scriptures that are difficult to obtain; it is simply that the road is treacherous and hard to travel.” “About thirty li west of here stands a mountain called the eight-hundred-li Yellow Wind Ridge, and many demons inhabit it.” “That is why I said the scriptures would be hard to obtain.” “Still, if this young reverend truly possesses all the abilities he claims, you may perhaps be able to pass.” The Pilgrim said, “Never fear, never fear.” “With old Monkey and this junior brother of mine here, no demon, whatever it may be, will dare provoke us.”

p.src: As they were speaking, the son came in with the food, set it on the table, and said, “Please partake of the meal.” Tripitaka joined his palms and began reciting the mealtime sutra. Bajie had already swallowed down one bowl. Before the elder had finished his few lines of scripture, the idiot had polished off three more bowls. The Pilgrim said, “What a meal-stuffing clod! You would think he had run into a starving ghost.” Old Wang was perceptive enough. Seeing how quickly Bajie ate, he said, “This reverend must be truly famished. Quickly, bring him more rice.” The idiot truly had an enormous appetite. Without once raising his head, he ate more than ten bowls in succession. Tripitaka and the Pilgrim each ate fewer than two bowls. The idiot did not stop but kept right on eating. Old Wang said, “We had no time to prepare any delicacies, so I dare not press you too earnestly, but please take another bite.” Tripitaka and the Pilgrim both said, “We have had enough.” Bajie said, “Old man, what are you prattling about? Who asked you to tell fortunes and talk of five lines and six lines?” “If there is rice, just keep bringing it.” In that one meal, the idiot consumed every scrap of food in the household, yet still said he was only half full. Only then did they clear away the utensils and arrange bamboo beds and plank pallets beneath the gatehouse for the travelers to sleep upon.

p.src: At daybreak the next morning, the Pilgrim went to saddle the horse while Bajie put the carrying pole in order. Old Wang again had his wife prepare refreshments and hot broth for them, and only after partaking did the three travelers offer their thanks and announce their departure. The old man said, “If you meet with any mishap along the road, be sure to return to my humble cottage.” The Pilgrim said, “Old man, do not talk such nonsense.” “We who have left the household never retrace our steps.” Thereupon they urged the horse onward, shouldered the luggage, and headed west.

p.src: Bajie stepped forward, seized the Pilgrim, and said, “Elder Brother, the wind is terribly strong. Let us find a good place to shelter for a while.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Brother, you are no good at all.” “If you hide whenever the wind blows hard, what will you do if you come face-to-face with a demon?” Bajie said, “Brother, have you never heard the saying, ‘Shun lust as you would an enemy, and shun wind as you would an arrow’?” “There is no shame in sheltering for a while.” The Pilgrim said, “Say no more. Let me catch a handful of this wind and smell it.” Bajie laughed. “Elder Brother, you are telling empty lies again. How could anyone catch the wind and smell it?” “Even if you caught it, it would slip through your fingers and escape.” The Pilgrim said, “Brother, you do not know that old Monkey has a method for catching wind.” What a Great Sage! He let the head of the gale pass, caught its trailing edge, and gave it a sniff. There was a certain rank odor to it. He said, “Sure enough, this is no wholesome wind. It does not smell like tiger wind; it must be a monster’s wind. There is unquestionably something strange about it.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, a brilliantly striped and ferocious tiger sprang from below the mountainside, tail tucked and hooves flying. Tripitaka was so terrified that he could not stay seated in his carved saddle. He somersaulted from the white horse and collapsed beside the road, his soul scattered and his wits utterly fled. Bajie dropped the luggage and whipped out his nine-pronged rake. p.src: He shouted, “Hold! Hold! I am none other than the vanguard officer serving under the Great King Yellow Wind. By our king’s strict command, I am patrolling this mountain to seize a few mortals as food to accompany his wine. Where have you monks come from, that you dare take up arms and wound me?” Bajie cursed him: “You vile beast! You plainly do not know who I am. We are no ordinary travelers, but disciples of Tripitaka, the imperial brother of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying by decree to worship the Buddha in the West and seek the scriptures. Make haste and withdraw elsewhere, clear the road, and do not alarm my master; then I shall spare your life. But if you run wild as before, I shall show no mercy when I raise my rake.” The fiend would hear no argument. He rushed forward, assumed a fighting stance, and clawed straight at Bajie’s face. Bajie hastily dodged aside, swung his rake, and struck. The monster, having no weapon in hand, turned and fled. Bajie pursued close behind. Reaching a jumble of rocks beneath the slope, the monster drew a pair of red-copper sabers, whirled them swiftly, and turned to meet him. Before the slope, the two charged back and forth, clashing fiercely in combat.

p.src: The Pilgrim drew his iron staff and shouted, “Take that!” At this, Bajie rallied his spirits, and the monster began to lose the fight. The Pilgrim said, “Do not spare him. We must catch him.” The two brandished rake and iron staff and chased him down the mountain. The monster, thrown into a panic, resorted to a cicada-shedding-its-shell trick. He rolled over and revealed his true form, once more becoming a fierce tiger. The Pilgrim and Bajie had no intention of letting him go. They chased the tiger, determined to destroy him root and branch. Seeing them draw near, the monster clawed open his breast, stripped off his hide, and spread it over the Crouching Tiger Rock. Slipping free in his true body, he transformed into a violent gust and went straight back to the road junction. There he suddenly saw their master reciting the Heart Sutra. Seizing him in one grasp, he rode the long wind and carried him away. Alas for Tripitaka: River Float was fated to endure many trials; hard indeed is the perfecting of merit within the gate of nirvana.

p.src: The monster carried the Tang Monk to the cave entrance and brought the wild wind to rest. To the gatekeeper he said, “Go report to the Great King that Tiger Vanguard, who guards the forward road, has captured a monk and awaits orders outside.” The cave lord issued an order to bring him in. With his two red-copper sabers tucked into his belt, Tiger Vanguard held the Tang Monk in both hands, advanced, and knelt, saying, “Great King, though this humble officer has little ability, I was graciously ordered to patrol the mountain. There I unexpectedly met a monk. He is the imperial brother of the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, the Dharma Master Tripitaka, journeying west to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. I captured him and offer him to Your Majesty as a modest meal.”

p.src: When the cave lord heard this, he started in alarm and said, “I once heard someone say that the Dharma Master Tripitaka is a divine monk sent by imperial decree from the Great Tang to fetch the scriptures. Among his disciples is one called Sun the Pilgrim, whose supernatural powers are vast and whose intelligence and strength are formidable. How were you able to capture him?” The vanguard replied, “He has two disciples. The first to come wielded a nine-pronged rake and had a long snout and enormous ears. The other wielded an iron staff with golden bands and had fiery eyes with golden pupils. They were hard upon me and pressing the fight when I used a cicada-shedding-its-shell stratagem to slip away. Finding an opening, I seized this monk and brought him as an offering to Your Majesty, as a humble token of my respect in the form of a meal.” The cave lord said, “We must not eat him yet.” The vanguard said, “Great King, is it not sheer folly to see food and refuse to eat it?” The cave lord replied, “You do not understand. Eating him would be no great matter, but I fear his two disciples will come to our door and make trouble. That would hardly be safe. For now, bind him to the Wind-Stilling Post in the rear garden. If after three or five days those two have not come to disturb us, then his body will be purged and clean, and we shall avoid any quarrel besides. Will we not then be free to do with him as we please? We may boil him, steam him, fry him, or sauté him, and take our leisurely pleasure without it being too late.” The vanguard was delighted. “Your Majesty plans deeply and looks far ahead. What you say is most reasonable.” He ordered, “Underlings, take him away.”

p.src: Seven or eight binding hands crowded forward from the side and carried off the Tang Monk. Like a hawk seizing a swallow, they trussed him tight with ropes. Ill-fated River Float longed for the Pilgrim; the divine monk in peril yearned for Wuneng. He cried, “My disciples! I know not on what mountain you are capturing monsters or where you are subduing fiends, while I have been taken by this demon and suffer such cruel harm. When shall we ever meet again? How bitter is my plight! If you come a little sooner, you may still save my life. But if you are much delayed, I assuredly cannot survive.” As he lamented, his tears fell like rain.

p.src: Now the Pilgrim and Bajie pursued the tiger down the slope, only to see it fall and lie flattened before a cliff. The Pilgrim raised his staff and struck with all his strength, but the shock only made his own hands ache. Bajie struck another blow with his rake, but its prongs sprang back as well. It proved to be nothing but a tiger skin draped over a Crouching Tiger Rock. The Pilgrim cried in alarm, “This is bad! This is bad! We have fallen for his trick!” Bajie asked, “What trick have we fallen for?” The Pilgrim said, “This is called the cicada-shedding-its-shell stratagem. He covered this place with his tiger skin, while he himself escaped. Let us go back at once and see to Master, lest he come to harm.” The two hurried back, but Tripitaka had already vanished. The Pilgrim shouted like thunder, “What are we to do? Master has already been captured and carried off by him.” Bajie took hold of the horse and, tears dripping from his eyes, cried, “Heavens! Heavens! Where can we go to find him?” The Pilgrim raised his head and said, “Do not cry. Do not cry. Tears will only blunt our fighting spirit. In any case, he can only be somewhere on this mountain. Let us search for him.”

p.src: Wukong straightened his robe, tightened his tiger-skin kilt, drew his staff, and charged up to the entrance. There he saw six great characters above the gate: “Yellow Wind Cave, Yellow Wind Ridge.” Planting his feet firmly in a T-shaped stance and gripping his staff, he shouted, “Monster! Send my master out at once, unless you want me to overturn your lair and flatten your dwelling!” Hearing this, the lesser demons were terrified. Trembling, they ran inside to report, “Your Majesty, disaster has struck!” The Yellow Wind Demon was seated within. “What is the matter?” he asked. A lesser demon replied, “Outside the cave stands a monk with a thunder-god’s snout and a hairy face. He is holding an enormous, thick iron staff and demanding his master back.” The cave lord was alarmed. He immediately summoned the Tiger Vanguard and said, “I sent you to patrol the mountain, and you should only have caught wild cattle, boars, fat deer, or foreign sheep. Why did you seize the Tang Monk and provoke his disciple into coming here to make trouble? What are we to do?” The Vanguard said, “Your Majesty, set your mind at ease and sleep soundly without worry. Though I am a poor warrior, I am willing to lead fifty troops outside, capture that fellow Sun Wukong, and add him to the feast.” The cave lord said, “Besides the commanders great and small, I have another five to seven hundred troops here. Choose as you please and take as many as you need. If only you can capture that Wukong, so that we may eat the monk’s flesh at our leisure, I will gladly swear brotherhood with you. But I fear that you may fail to catch him and instead be wounded yourself. Do not blame me then.” The tiger demon said, “Do not worry, do not worry. Just wait until I return.”

p.src: Sure enough, he mustered fifty strong lesser demons. With drums beating and banners waving, he strapped on two red-copper sabers, bounded out through the gate, and cried fiercely, “Where did you come from, monkey monk, and what makes you dare raise such a clamor here?” Wukong cursed him: “You flayed beast! You used some trick of shedding your skin to carry off my master, and now you turn around and ask what I am doing? Send my master out unharmed at once, and I will still spare your life.” The tiger demon said, “I was the one who captured your master, and he is to make a meal for my king. If you know what is good for you, go back. Otherwise, we shall capture you and add you to the feast as well. Why take one and let another go free?” Hearing this, Wukong flew into a rage. His steel-hard teeth ground together with a grating sound, and his fiery golden eyes opened round and wide. Brandishing his iron staff, he shouted, “What powers do you possess, that you dare boast so outrageously? Do not flee—take this staff!” The Vanguard hastily raised his sabers to parry the blow. This was indeed a vicious battle. Each displayed his formidable prowess—a fine fight it was:
